paras.t: On a frozen island halfway between Norway and the North Pole, a concrete wedge juts from a mountainside. Inside the mountain lies the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, a facility that
stores, and preserves, more than one million seed samples
from crops around the world.
Conceived as a backup drive for global agriculture,
the vault guards crop diversity against war, disaster, and neglect.
The vault's location was chosen with care. Svalbard's permafrost keeps the seeds frozen
even when the electricity goes out and the generators stop.
The islands are remote enough to discourage casual visitors, yet they are governed by a stable democracy. In 2015, researchers made the first withdrawal from the vault, sending seeds
to reestablish a gene bank that had been housed in Aleppo, Syria.
Each arriving sample is sealed in a moisture-proof pouch and shelved in one of three chilly halls.
The seeds themselves remain the property of the depositors, and Norway claims no ownership over them.
Despite the vault's nickname — the “doomsday vault” —
its managers say the vault is more about hope than about the end of the world.
Still, the vault has faced challenges. In 2017, meltwater from unusually warm weather
breached the entrance tunnel, it prompted
engineers to waterproof the passage.
No seeds were harmed, but the incident reminded the world that even a fortress in the Arctic
can't escape a changing climate.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
stores and preserves more than one million seed samples
stores, and preserves more than, one million seed samples
stores and preserves, more than one million seed samples
questions.explain: “Stores and preserves” is a compound verb, which takes no comma, and “more than one million” needs none either. Every comma in A, C, and D wrongly splits the verb or the quantity.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
Conceiving it as a backup drive for global agriculture,
It conceived as a backup drive for global agriculture,
Having been conceived as a backup drive for global agriculture and
questions.explain: The opening participle “conceived” correctly modifies “the vault.” B dangles (a vault cannot conceive); C is missing its helping verb; D leaves the phrase with no main clause to attach to.

questions.stem: Which choice is least redundant in context?
options: No Change
even if the power fails.
even when the electrical power goes out.
even if the power fails and stops working.
questions.explain: “Even if the power fails” says it once. A and C restate the outage in extra words; D repeats “fails” as “stops working.”

questions.stem: The writer wants to explain why the first withdrawal mattered. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
to test whether decade-old seeds could still sprout.
to celebrate the vault's tenth anniversary.
to count how many samples the vault holds.
questions.explain: Reestablishing a destroyed gene bank shows the vault fulfilling its purpose in the real world. B narrows it to an experiment, C invents an anniversary, and D reduces it to an inventory count.

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?
options: Kept, because it describes how seeds are packaged for storage.
Kept, because it clarifies who owns the deposited seeds.
Deleted, because it repeats information about Norway's climate.
Deleted, because it lists countries that deposited seeds.
questions.explain: The sentence settles ownership — depositors keep it, Norway claims none — which nothing else states. A describes the previous sentence, while C and D misread the content entirely.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively maintains the essay's formal tone?
options: No Change
its managers swear the vault is about hope, not doom.
its managers maintain that the facility embodies optimism rather than disaster.
its managers say the vault gives hope vibes instead of doom stuff.
questions.explain: “Maintain,” “embodies,” and “rather than” match the essay's formal register. A is wordy and casual, while B and D use slang (“swear,” “doom,” “vibes”).

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
breached the entrance tunnel, prompting
breached the entrance tunnel, and prompting
breached the entrance tunnel; prompting
questions.explain: The original joins two independent clauses with a comma — a splice. “Prompting” turns the second half into a participial phrase; C is ungrammatical and D strands a fragment after the semicolon.

questions.stem: Which choice maintains the essay's formal tone while stating the consequence?
options: No Change
is not immune to a changing climate.
has no shelter from a changing climate.
cannot hide from a changing climate.
questions.explain: “Immune to” is the precise formal idiom. A leans on a contraction and casual phrasing, while C and D are colloquial.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay: *News of the breach traveled around the world within days.* The sentence would most logically be placed at:
options: Point A in Paragraph 2.
Point B in Paragraph 3.
Point C in Paragraph 4.
Point D in Paragraph 4.
questions.explain: The news belongs immediately after the breach is described at Point C. Points A and B come before the incident, and Point D follows the closing reflection on climate.

questions.stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence: *Schoolchildren in Longyearbyen sometimes tour the vault's entrance.* Should the writer make this addition?
options: Yes, because it shows that local residents take pride in the vault.
Yes, because it proves the vault welcomes visitors of all ages.
No, because it shifts focus from the vault's global mission to local tourism.
No, because it fails to name the children's school.
questions.explain: The essay closes on the vault's global purpose and climate vulnerability; a local-tour detail pulls away from that mission. A overreads pride, B overclaims access, and D faults a missing detail that was never needed.

paras.t: On autumn evenings over Rome, the sky begins to boil. Thousands of starlings wheel and dive in a single rippling cloud, a performance scientists call a murmuration.
No single bird leads the flock, and the birds react to their neighbors with astonishing speed.
Each bird tracks about seven neighbors, adjusting its course in fractions of a second. The result is a shape that
looks like it was choreographed, it shifts too fast for any choreographer to plan.
Watching a murmuration
is pretty cool because the birds make awesome shapes.
Biologists believe the displays
confuse predators such as falcons,
which struggle to track one bird among thousands. Rome's starlings gather above the city's warm rooftops each winter,
drawn by the heat rising from the streets below.
At dawn they scatter to feed in the countryside, returning each evening to perform again.

questions.stem: The writer wants to explain how the flock stays coordinated. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
Each bird simply follows the one directly in front of it.
The birds take turns leading for a few seconds each.
Scientists steer the flock with recorded calls.
questions.explain: No leader plus fast neighbor-reactions is exactly the decentralized coordination the passage describes. B and C invent leadership schemes the sentence denies, and D invents human control.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
looks choreographed, shifting too fast for any choreographer to plan.
looks like choreography, and shifting too fast for any choreographer to plan.
they look choreographed, shifting too fast for anyone to plan.
questions.explain: The original is a comma splice. “Shifting” makes the second half a participial phrase attached to the shape; C is ungrammatical after “and,” and D gives “they” no clear antecedent.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively maintains the essay's tone?
options: No Change
is captivating, as the flock sculpts fleeting shapes.
is nice since the birds fly around a lot.
is fun because the shapes are sick.
questions.explain: “Captivating” and “sculpts” match the essay's elevated register. A is chatty, C is flat, and D is slang.

questions.stem: The writer wants to state the leading theory about the murmuration's function. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
entertain tourists visiting Rome.
help the birds find food after sunset.
signal bedtime to young birds.
questions.explain: Predator confusion is the theory biologists actually propose here. Tourism, feeding, and bedtime signals appear nowhere in the passage.

questions.stem: The writer is considering revising the underlined portion to *lured by the city's deceptive glow.* Should the writer make this revision?
options: Yes, because the revision adds vivid language suited to the evening scene.
Yes, because the revision explains why the starlings leave at dawn.
No, because “lured” and “deceptive” wrongly imply the warmth is a trap.
No, because the original fails to mention the rooftops.
questions.explain: “Lured” and “deceptive” smuggle in menace the passage never suggests; the neutral “drawn” fits the plain description. A praises vividness that distorts meaning, B answers the wrong question, and D faults a detail already present.

paras.t: On a wall in a library in Istanbul, a thirteenth-century map shows the world as a circle, with Jerusalem at its center.
This mappa mundi, like most medieval European maps, was less a tool for navigation than a diagram of theological geography.
Maps of that era arranged continents to reflect religious narratives rather than physical distances.
The modern idea of a map as a scaled representation of terrain emerged during the Renaissance.
In 1569, the Flemish geographer Gerardus Mercator published a world map that
distorted landmasses near the poles so that compass bearings could be drawn as straight lines.
Sailors valued the projection, it simplified navigation by turning curved routes into straight bearings.
By the eighteenth century, governments began funding systematic surveys to define borders and tax territories.
The French cartographer César-François Cassini spent four decades mapping France at a consistent scale.
His teams produced the first topographic map of an entire country.
Such efforts required surveyors, mathematicians, and engravers to work together in the field for years.
Today, satellite imagery and geographic information systems have replaced hand-drawn surveys, yet the core challenge remains the same:
representing a curved surface on a flat page without losing essential information.
Digital maps update in real time, but they still rely on the same projection principles Mercator codified centuries ago.
The ethics of mapping have also evolved, however, challenges remain.
For example, indigenous communities now press for sacred sites to be removed from public maps.
As technology advances, cartographers must balance accuracy with responsibility.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
This mappa mundi, like most medieval European maps was, less a tool for navigation than a diagram of theological geography.
This mappa mundi like most medieval European maps, was less a tool for navigation than a diagram of theological geography.
This mappa mundi like most medieval European maps was, less a tool for navigation than a diagram of theological geography.
questions.explain: The aside "like most medieval European maps" is non-essential and must be closed off by paired commas. B shifts the second comma to the wrong spot, C and D remove the first comma, and D strips both — each lets the aside bleed into the main clause.

questions.stem: The writer wants to identify Mercator and introduce his achievement in language consistent with the essay's formal tone. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
In 1569, Gerardus Mercator, a map guy from Flanders, published a world map that
In 1569, the mapmaker Gerardus Mercator, who came from what is now Belgium, published a world map that
In 1569, the famous Flemish geographer Gerardus Mercator published a world map that
questions.explain: "The Flemish geographer" states Mercator's nationality and profession in the essay's formal register. B's slang, C's wordy detour, and D's unsupported "famous" all weaken the introduction.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
Sailors valued the projection; it simplified navigation by turning curved routes into straight bearings.
Sailors valued the projection it simplified navigation by turning curved routes into straight bearings.
Sailors, valuing the projection, it simplified navigation by turning curved routes into straight bearings.
questions.explain: The two complete clauses must be joined by a semicolon, as in B. A splices them with a comma alone, C fuses them with no punctuation, and D strands "valuing the projection" so it appears to modify "it" instead of "sailors."

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?
options: Kept, because it names a concrete example of the government-funded surveys introduced in this paragraph.
Kept, because it proves that France produced better maps than any other country.
Deleted, because the essay should concentrate on Mercator's projection, not on later mapmakers.
Deleted, because Cassini's project was funded privately rather than by the government.
questions.explain: Cassini's four-decade survey is exactly the kind of systematic, government-funded mapping the paragraph introduces. B overstates the comparison, C ignores that the essay is tracing cartography's broader history, and D contradicts the sentence's clear statement of government funding.

questions.stem: Which choice most precisely describes what Cassini's project accomplished while maintaining the essay's formal tone?
options: No Change
His teams made a really accurate map of the whole country.
His teams created a drawing of France.
His teams produced the first topographic map of an entire country, showing all its mountains and valleys.
questions.explain: "Topographic map of an entire country" is the precise, formal phrasing. B slips into casual language, C loses the technical meaning of "topographic," and D restates what "topographic" already conveys.

questions.stem: The writer wants to state the enduring challenge that modern mapmakers still face. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
drawing a map that shows every road, river, and boundary on Earth at once.
making maps that will look perfect to anyone who sees them.
representing a curved surface on a flat page completely and perfectly, preserving all information without any loss whatsoever.
questions.explain: A states the problem precisely: projecting a curved globe onto a flat page without losing essential data. B misstates the challenge, C is vague and informal, and D pads the idea with redundant emphasis.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay: *With every advance, the question of what maps should show grows more complicated.* The sentence would most logically be placed at:
options: Point A in Paragraph 1.
Point B in Paragraph 2.
Point C in Paragraph 3.
Point D in Paragraph 4.
questions.explain: Point D follows the statement that map ethics have grown complicated, and the added sentence's general reflection is then illustrated by the sacred-sites example that follows. Points A, B, and C all occur before that ethical discussion exists.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively connects the sentence to the essay's earlier discussion of Mercator's projection?
options: No Change
Digital maps update in real time, but they still rely on the same basic principles of mapmaking.
Digital maps update in real time, so they have left Mercator's principles behind.
Digital maps update in real time, but they still rely on the projection principles that Mercator codified back in 1569.
questions.explain: "Still rely on the same projection principles Mercator codified" ties today's digital maps back to the sixteenth-century projection described in Paragraph 2. B severs that link, C reverses the passage's meaning, and D repeats the date with a casual "back in."

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
The ethics of mapping have also evolved; however, challenges remain.
The ethics of mapping have also evolved however, challenges remain.
The ethics of mapping have also evolved, however challenges remain.
questions.explain: "However" is a conjunctive adverb joining two complete clauses, so a semicolon must separate them, as in B. A splices the clauses with commas alone, C fuses them with no punctuation, and D strands "however" without the comma it requires.

questions.stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence: *Some parks now display both indigenous and colonial place names on their maps.* Should the writer make this addition?
options: Yes, because it offers a concrete example of the ethical balancing the paragraph describes.
Yes, because it proves that all governments now respect indigenous traditions.
No, because it introduces parks, a topic unrelated to mapmaking.
No, because it contradicts the claim that mapping has become more ethical.
questions.explain: The added sentence illustrates how modern maps balance indigenous and colonial place names — precisely the ethical complexity the paragraph introduces. B overgeneralizes to "all governments," C ignores that parks appear on maps, and D misreads the example as contradicting ethical progress.

paras.t: On a July afternoon, one side of Elm Street can feel ten degrees cooler than the other. A row of mature oaks on the shady side
shade the sidewalk and cool the air.
Cities should plant far more street trees, because the benefits of shade, cleaner air, and stormwater control outweigh the costs of planting and care.
The evidence for planting is strong.
In one study, shaded streets measured up to nine degrees cooler than bare streets at midday.
Shade is only the beginning, moreover, leaves trap dust and absorb gases.
Trees also slow stormwater, giving drains time to keep up during heavy rain.
Critics point to cracked sidewalks and clogged gutters. Roots can buckle pavement, and falling limbs can damage cars.
Yet these problems shrink when cities choose appropriate species and give roots room to grow.
In other words, the costs critics cite are manageable, while the benefits compound every year.
The choice is ultimately a practical one.
A city that plants trees today gives its residents decades of shade, cleaner air, and cooler summers.
Neighborhood groups can request plantings, and councils can fund maintenance year after year.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
shades the sidewalk and cools the air.
shade the sidewalk and cools the air.
shading the sidewalk and cooling the air.
questions.explain: The subject is the singular noun "row" — cross out the prepositional phrase "of mature oaks on the shady side" to see it. B gives both verbs the singular form. A and C use the plural "shade," and D leaves the sentence with no main verb at all.

questions.stem: The writer wants to state the essay's central argument in formal language. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
Cities should plant a ton more street trees because trees are awesome and concrete stinks.
Trees are among the oldest living organisms on Earth.
Cities should plant more oaks on Elm Street.
questions.explain: A states the position plainly — plant far more street trees — and previews the essay's reasons: shade, cleaner air, stormwater control, weighed against costs. B slips into slang, C is true but off-thesis, and D narrows the argument to one species on one street.

questions.stem: The writer wants to support the claim that trees cool streets with concrete evidence. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
Trees are especially beautiful in autumn.
Some pedestrians actually prefer the sunny side of the street.
Researchers counted every tree on four streets before lunch.
questions.explain: A cites a measured result — nine degrees cooler at midday — that directly proves the cooling claim. B praises autumn looks, C notes a preference that undercuts nothing and proves nothing, and D reports a procedural detail with no finding attached.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
Shade is only the beginning; moreover, leaves trap dust and absorb gases.
Shade is only the beginning moreover leaves trap dust and absorb gases.
Shade is only the beginning, moreover leaves trap dust and absorb gases.
questions.explain: "Moreover" is a conjunctive adverb joining two complete clauses, so it needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it, as in B. A splices the clauses with commas alone, C fuses them with no punctuation, and D drops the comma that must follow "moreover."

questions.stem: Which choice provides the most logical transition, given that the sentence adds another benefit of street trees?
options: No Change
Trees however slow stormwater, giving drains time to keep up during heavy rain.
Trees for example slow stormwater, giving drains time to keep up during heavy rain.
Trees instead slow stormwater, giving drains time to keep up during heavy rain.
questions.explain: The sentence adds a further benefit, so the additive transition "also" is correct. "However" and "instead" signal contrast or substitution, and "for example" signals an illustration — none of which fits a new item in the list of benefits.

questions.stem: The writer wants to answer the critics' objections with a practical solution. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
Yet trees are much prettier than sidewalks, so critics should look on the bright side.
Yet critics should stop complaining and let the city do its job.
Yet sidewalks crack for many reasons, so trees are hardly the problem.
questions.explain: A meets the objections head-on: proper species selection and room for roots shrink the damage critics cite. B answers with an aesthetic opinion, C dismisses the critics rudely, and D deflects blame onto other causes without offering any solution.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay: *A single mature oak can intercept thousands of gallons of rainfall each year.* The sentence would most logically be placed at:
options: Point A in Paragraph 1.
Point B in Paragraph 2.
Point C in Paragraph 3.
Point D in Paragraph 4.
questions.explain: Point B sits beside the paragraph's evidence on cooling, air quality, and stormwater — the rainfall statistic belongs with that supporting detail. Point A precedes the evidence, while Points C and D come after the essay has moved on to objections and conclusions.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively concludes the paragraph's rebuttal by returning to the essay's central argument?
options: No Change
In other words, trees are nicer than concrete.
In other words, the benefits critics cite are manageable, while the costs compound every year.
In other words, everyone should stop arguing and plant trees.
questions.explain: A restates the thesis in the paragraph's terms — manageable costs against compounding benefits. B is vague and casual, C reverses the meaning by swapping costs and benefits, and D issues an informal command instead of an argument.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
A city that plants trees today gives it's residents decades of shade, cleaner air, and cooler summers.
A city that plants trees today gives their residents decades of shade, cleaner air, and cooler summers.
A city that plants trees today gives its' residents decades of shade, cleaner air, and cooler summers.
questions.explain: The antecedent "city" is singular, so the possessive pronoun must be the singular "its." B uses the contraction "it is," C uses the plural "their," and D uses "its'," which is not a word in English.

questions.stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence: *Volunteers who water young trees through their first two summers dramatically raise survival rates.* Should the writer make this addition?
options: Yes, because it names a specific action that helps the plantings described in the paragraph survive.
Yes, because it proves that volunteers can replace city funding entirely.
No, because it shifts focus from street trees to houseplants.
No, because it suggests young trees need no care at all.
questions.explain: Watering young trees is the concrete follow-through the paragraph's call for plantings and maintenance requires. B overclaims that volunteers can replace funding, C misreads the subject as houseplants, and D reverses the sentence's meaning.

paras.t: Every December, my grandmother
turned her small kitchen into a dumpling factory.
By noon, the counters were dusted white with flour, and the radio played carols over the hiss of the kettle.
The air smelled of ginger and scallion, sharp and warm at once.
At first, she showed
my sister and I
how to pleat the edges without tearing the wrappers. Mine split open every time.
Later, my sister's sealed shut on the first try.
Grandmother laughed and rolled another wrapper, a fresh one, for me to try again.
By midafternoon, my fingers ached, and half my dumplings still resembled small, lumpy envelopes.
The radio had moved on to the news by then.
Still, I kept pleating, and somewhere around the twentieth wrapper my thumbs finally learned the rhythm.
Thinking of her every time the ginger hits the hot oil, the scent fills my kitchen with memory.
Some lessons arrive not as instructions but as afternoons.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
turns her small kitchen into a dumpling factory.
had turned her small kitchen into a dumpling factory and will turn it again.
turning her small kitchen into a dumpling factory.
questions.explain: The memoir is told in the past tense, so the simple past "turned" is correct. B shifts into the present, C tangles past perfect with future, and D leaves the sentence with no main verb at all.

questions.stem: Which choice best preserves the narrator's vivid sensory voice?
options: No Change
The air smelled okay.
The air had a smell.
The air smelled of ginger and scallion, which are ingredients.
questions.explain: In a narrative, vivid sensory detail is a strength: "sharp and warm at once" lets the reader smell the kitchen. B and C flatten the image into near-nothing, and D turns the image into a flat definition.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
my sister and me
my sister and myself
we
questions.explain: The pronoun is the object of "showed," so it must take the objective case: "me." A uses the nominative "I," C misuses the reflexive "myself," and D replaces two people with a pronoun that cannot serve as the object here.

questions.stem: Which choice most accurately places the sister's success in time, given that both children are practicing in the same afternoon session?
options: No Change
Meanwhile, my sister's sealed shut on the first try.
The next year, my sister's sealed shut on the first try.
Eventually, my sister's sealed shut on the first try.
questions.explain: Her success happens during the same session, so "meanwhile" correctly marks simultaneity. "Later," "the next year," and "eventually" all falsely push her first-try success into the future — and "eventually" contradicts "the first try."

questions.stem: Which choice is least redundant in context?
options: No Change
Grandmother laughed and rolled another wrapper for me to try again.
Grandmother laughed and rolled another wrapper, a fresh new one, for me to try again.
Grandmother laughed and rolled another wrapper, which was a wrapper and fresh, for me to try again.
questions.explain: "Another" already means one more and fresh, so B says it once. A restates it as "a fresh one," C doubles it as "a fresh new one," and D spells out the redundancy word by word.

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?
options: Kept, because it shows that the afternoon is passing.
Kept, because it explains the pleating technique.
Deleted, because it breaks the paragraph's focus on the narrator's practice with an unrelated detail.
Deleted, because it repeats the description of the flour.
questions.explain: The paragraph is about aching fingers and lumpy envelopes — the narrator's struggle to learn. The radio bulletin adds nothing to that focus, and the time-passing detail is already carried by "by midafternoon." A praises a redundant time marker, B misreads the content, and D misidentifies what the sentence says.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay: *My sister still brags that her first dumpling was perfect.* The sentence would most logically be placed at:
options: Point A in Paragraph 1.
Point B in Paragraph 2.
Point C in Paragraph 3.
Point D in Paragraph 4.
questions.explain: Point B sits beside the sibling-contrast moment — her first-try success against the narrator's split wrappers — so the brag completes that scene. Point A comes before the sister even appears, and Points C and D arrive after the scene has moved on to practice and reflection.

questions.stem: The writer wants to show the narrator's persistence paying off. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
Still, I kept pleating, and I ate three dumplings.
Still, I kept pleating, and my sister left the kitchen.
Still, I kept pleating, and the radio played another carol.
questions.explain: A delivers the payoff: the thumbs "finally learned the rhythm" around the twentieth wrapper. B detours into snacking, C follows the sister out of the scene, and D returns to the radio without resolving the learning arc.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
Thinking of her every time the ginger hits the hot oil, I breathe in memory with the scent.
Thinking of her every time the ginger hits the hot oil, memory is breathed in by me.
Thinking of her every time the ginger hits the hot oil and the scent fills my kitchen with memory.
questions.explain: An opening participle must modify the subject, and only B supplies "I" as the one thinking. In A the scent absurdly does the thinking, in C memory does, and D fuses the participial phrase to a clause with "and," leaving the grammar broken.

questions.stem: The writer wants an ending that captures the memory's lasting meaning. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
Dumplings are a traditional food in many cultures.
My sister still pleats faster than I do.
Everyone should learn to cook before college.
questions.explain: A closes the memoir's past-and-present arc with reflection: the lesson was the afternoon itself. B turns encyclopedic, C revives the sibling rivalry on the wrong note, and D preaches advice the essay never set out to give.

paras.t: When a honeybee colony outgrows its hive, roughly half the bees swarm out with the old queen. Each returning scout reports three pieces of
information: direction, distance, and quality.
The scout advertises her find by dancing: the livelier the waggle dance, the better the site.
Advertised sites then compete for supporters.
In experiments, the swarm eventually dances for one site alone, abandoning weaker candidates.
Gradually, weaker dances fade as scouts switch allegiance to stronger ones.
A scout inspects a cavity,
measuring its volume, and dances with matching enthusiasm.
Biologist Thomas Seeley tested the process by offering swarms five nest boxes of different quality.
He painted the boxes different colors so that scouts could tell them apart.
Time after time, the swarm chose the best box.
Seeley concluded that no bee is in charge:
the decision emerges from hundreds of independent inspections.
The
bees' ability
to choose well without a leader has inspired engineers designing robot swarms.
Democracy, it turns out, is older than voting.
Researchers now study whether other social insects decide the same way.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
information; direction, distance, and quality.
information, direction, distance, and quality.
information direction, distance, and quality.
questions.explain: The colon correctly follows a complete sentence and introduces the list of three items. A semicolon cannot introduce a list, a comma splices the list into the clause, and no punctuation fuses them together.

questions.stem: The writer wants to explain how scouts communicate the quality of a site. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
The scout celebrates her find by dancing happily.
The scout rests after her long flight.
The scout dances to entertain the swarm.
questions.explain: A encodes the communication rule precisely: livelier dance means better site. B is vague and casual, C contradicts the reporting behavior, and D misreads the dance as entertainment.

questions.stem: The writer wants to give evidence that competition among sites ends in consensus. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
In experiments, the swarm eventually dances beautifully.
In experiments, the swarm eventually visits every site in person.
In experiments, the swarm eventually forgets all the sites.
questions.explain: A states the observed outcome — one site alone, weaker candidates abandoned — which is exactly consensus. B praises the dancing, C wrongly sends the whole swarm visiting, and D claims the opposite of the finding.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically continues the paragraph's account of a contest unfolding over time?
options: No Change
However, weaker dances fade as scouts switch allegiance to stronger ones.
For example, weaker dances fade as scouts switch allegiance to stronger ones.
Instead, weaker dances fade as scouts switch allegiance to stronger ones.
questions.explain: "Gradually" marks the slow shift of support as the contest unfolds. "However" and "instead" signal a contrast or substitution that is not happening, and "for example" wrongly frames the next stage as a mere illustration.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
measures its volume, and dances with matching enthusiasm.
to measure its volume, and dances with matching enthusiasm.
measuring its volume, and to dance with matching enthusiasm.
questions.explain: The three verbs in the series — "inspects," "measures," "dances" — must share the same form. A mixes a participle into the series, C mixes an infinitive, and D mixes both.

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?
options: Kept, because it explains how scouts distinguished the boxes in the experiment.
Kept, because it proves that bees see color.
Deleted, because it repeats the boxes' dimensions.
Deleted, because the boxes play no role in the experiment.
questions.explain: The painted colors are the method detail that lets readers trust the result: scouts could tell the boxes apart. B overclaims proof about bee vision, C misreads colors as dimensions, and D denies the boxes' central role.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay: *A scout may visit a dozen cavities before dancing for her favorite.* The sentence would most logically be placed at:
options: Point A in Paragraph 1.
Point B in Paragraph 2.
Point C in Paragraph 3.
Point D in Paragraph 4.
questions.explain: Point A sits beside the introduction of scouting and the dance, so the detail about visiting cavities belongs there. Point B covers the debate phase, Point C the experiment, and Point D the closing reflection — all after scouting is established.

questions.stem: The writer wants to state Seeley's finding about leaderless decision-making. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
the queen picks the site alone.
the loudest dancer becomes the leader.
the scouts vote by secret ballot.
questions.explain: A states the finding exactly: no bee in charge, the choice emerging from many inspections. B contradicts the waiting queen, C invents a leader the passage denies, and D imports a human voting ritual bees do not use.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
The bee's ability to choose well without a leader has inspired engineers designing robot swarms.
The bees's ability to choose well without a leader has inspired engineers designing robot swarms.
The bees ability to choose well without a leader has inspired engineers designing robot swarms.
questions.explain: The ability belongs to many bees, so the plural possessive "bees'" is correct. B makes it one bee's ability, C uses a malformed possessive, and D drops the apostrophe entirely.

questions.stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence: *Engineers have already tested swarms of small robots that map collapsed buildings.* Should the writer make this addition?
options: Yes, because it gives a concrete example of the robot research the paragraph introduces.
Yes, because it proves that robots will soon replace honeybees.
No, because it shifts focus from honeybees to astronomy.
No, because it denies that engineers study bee behavior.
questions.explain: Mapping robots are the concrete payoff of the bio-inspired engineering the paragraph introduces. B overclaims replacement, C misreads robots as astronomy, and D reverses the sentence's meaning.

tests.title: In Defense of the Public Library

passages.title: In Defense of the Public Library

paras.t: On any weekday afternoon, the downtown library hums with more life than most coffee shops.
Cities should fund their public libraries generously, because no other institution offers free knowledge, free shelter, and free community to everyone.
The collection,
that spans three floors, holds
more than a million items.
The reasons begin with access.
In one year, patrons borrowed four million items, from novels to power drills.
Beyond books, the library lends tools, instruments, and internet hotspots.
The librarians who run job workshops, language classes, and summer reading programs
, deserve
more credit than they receive.
Skeptics argue that search engines have made libraries obsolete. Why fund buildings, they ask, when every answer fits in a pocket?
Yet a search engine cannot teach a child to read, help a newcomer fill out a job application, or give a teenager a safe place to study.
In short, the internet delivers information while the library delivers people the skills and shelter to use it.
Branches that stay open late serve their neighborhoods
more effectively than
branches that close at five.
Councils facing tight budgets should treat library hours as essential services, not optional extras.

questions.stem: The writer wants to state the essay's central argument in formal language. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
Cities should give libraries a ton of money because libraries are awesome and everything else is boring.
Books have existed for thousands of years.
Cities should fund the downtown library's coffee shop.
questions.explain: A states the position plainly — fund libraries generously — and previews the essay's case: knowledge, shelter, and community, free to all. B slips into slang, C is true but off-thesis, and D narrows the argument to a coffee shop.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
which spans three floors, holds
that spans three floors holds
which spans three floors holds
questions.explain: The clause is non-essential — there is one collection — so it needs "which" with paired commas. "That" cannot take commas, C's version implies several collections, and D drops the closing comma.

questions.stem: The writer wants to show the remarkable breadth of library lending with concrete evidence. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
In one year, patrons whispered quietly.
In one year, the roof was repainted.
In one year, every patron borrowed exactly one book.
questions.explain: A spans novels to power drills — four million items — proving breadth directly. B notes behavior that proves nothing, C reports an irrelevant repair, and D invents a false precision that shrinks the claim.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically widens the paragraph's scope from books to the library's other offerings?
options: No Change
However, the library lends tools, instruments, and internet hotspots.
In conclusion, the library lends tools, instruments, and internet hotspots.
Instead, the library lends tools, instruments, and internet hotspots.
questions.explain: "Beyond books" correctly widens the scope to further offerings. "However" and "instead" signal a contrast that is not happening, and "in conclusion" misplaces a finale in the middle of the essay.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
deserve
they deserve
; deserve
questions.explain: A single comma must never separate a subject from its verb, so B removes the intruding comma. C creates a double subject, and D strands the verb behind a semicolon with no clause to join.

questions.stem: The writer wants to answer the skeptics by naming things libraries do that a phone cannot. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: No Change
Yet search engines are faster than any librarian.
Yet skeptics should stop asking questions.
Yet libraries should become coffee shops.
questions.explain: A lists three irreplaceable human services — teaching reading, aiding job seekers, sheltering teenagers — that no search engine performs. B concedes the skeptics' point, C dismisses them rudely, and D abandons the library's mission.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay: *Retirees play chess at one table while toddlers hear stories at another.* The sentence would most logically be placed at:
options: Point A in Paragraph 1.
Point B in Paragraph 2.
Point C in Paragraph 3.
Point D in Paragraph 4.
questions.explain: Point A sits beside the opening portrait of the library's lively afternoon, so the chess-and-story-time scene belongs there. Points B, C, and D come after the essay has moved on to evidence, objections, and budgets.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively concludes the paragraph's rebuttal by returning to the essay's central argument?
options: No Change
In short, information is everywhere.
In short, the library delivers people more information than the internet.
In short, libraries are basically free bookstores.
questions.explain: A restates the thesis in the paragraph's terms: information versus the skills and shelter to use it. B concedes the skeptics' case, C contradicts the paragraph's own distinction, and D shrinks the library to a bookstore.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: No Change
more effective than
most effectively than
effectively than
questions.explain: The adverb "effectively" must modify the verb "serve," and comparing two groups needs the comparative "more" with "than." B uses the adjective form, C mixes a superlative with "than," and D drops the required "more."

questions.stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence: *One branch that restored evening hours saw attendance double within a year.* Should the writer make this addition?
options: Yes, because it gives concrete evidence that evening hours draw readers.
Yes, because it proves that every budget problem has been solved.
No, because it shifts focus from libraries to museums.
No, because it denies that hours affect attendance.
questions.explain: Doubled attendance is the concrete payoff the paragraph's call to protect hours requires. B overclaims a universal budget fix, C misreads branches as museums, and D reverses the sentence's meaning.
